claims.claim: But does not identify a lead agency to consolidate the reports or synthesize government-wide findings.
claims.sourceSpan: by striking paragraph (2) and inserting the following:
claims.note: The bill's new IG-report structure adds no consolidation mechanism — accurate as to THIS bill. Caveat for the verifier: preexisting FFATA Sec 6(b) (in the registered ref usc-31-6101) already directs the Comptroller General, 'after a review of the reports submitted under subsection (a),' to make a government-wide comparison report; the bill does not amend 6(b), so a government-wide synthesis mechanism already exists in underlying law. Non-material; gap is analytically defensible. Sonnet verify (observation b): confirmed 6(b) text in usc-31-6101.txt — but 6(b)(2)'s own deadline is 'not later than 30 months after the date on which the Director and the Secretary issue guidance... under section 4(c)(1), and every 2 years thereafter UNTIL the date that is 4 years after the date on which the first report is submitted under this subsection.' That guidance was due within 1 year of the 2014 DATA Act (4(c)(1)), so 6(b)'s recurring-report window (~30 months after ~2015 guidance, running 4 years past the first report) appears to have already sunset around 2021-2022 — years before this bill's 2025/2026 enactment, and with no reactivation anywhere in this bill's text. RULING: NOT misleading/material — if anything the gap is UNDERSTATED, not overstated: the 'existing' 6(b) mechanism the finder cites as a counterweight is itself time-limited and not shown current, while the bill's new Sec 6(a) IG-report cycle runs a full 10 years from enactment (through ~2036) with nothing in the bill tying it back to a live government-wide synthesis report. gaps[2] stands as written; no flag added, verdict remains SUPPORTED.

claims.claim: Ms. Ernst (R-IA, bioguide E000295, Senate) said: 'Taxpayers deserve to know how the money they send to Washington is being spent. For 20 years now, the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act has required unclassified government spending to be put online in a searchable public website, USAspending.gov. This allows taxpayers to review the receipts for themselves.'
